Tokyo, July 18.
A preliminary investigation shows that Japan's and America's views in China are fully in accord.

It is understood that during the course of a conference on July 16 between Mr. Austen Chamberlain and the French, Japanese and American ambassadors it was intimated that a purely judicial enquiry will be instituted in connection with the Shanghai incidents of May 31 and that the British Government will act in accordance with its findings. A general agreement was also reached in the desirability of convening the tariff Conference provided by the Washington Treaty but the date was left open. Also there was no difference of opinion concerning the duty of the Powers signatory to the Washington Treaties to undertake the earliest possible general enquiry into the question of extraterritorialism in China.

Note issued on the subject of disputes between the Shanghai municipality and the Diplomatic Corps at Peking with reference to enquiry into the Shanghai disorders, emphasises the loyalty of the each Minister to China to his leagues, and recalls that the International Commission has failed to reconcile the differences of these delegation and the Shanghai Municipality, and has reported that the Diplomatic Corps of Peking, which unanimously im-ad-certain sanctions to which the municipality refused to submit, forever, the British Minister had the notification of the plans to the Chinese Governance and the negotiations with Chinese Government for the treatment of the incidents thus impossible.

The India Manufacturers Association, representing ninety-five per cent. of the British manufacturers of rubber articles, has issued a manifesto protesting against the continuance of the operation of the Stevenson scheme and the present form for the restriction of the exports of crude rubber from Malay and Ceylon, and demanding that the scheme be abolished or so drastically amended that it will provide quick releases as and when the price of rubber goes beyond the limits aimed at by the scheme.

At Mr. Coolidge's suggestion a delegation representing American rubber interests has interviewed the Secretary of State, Mr. Kellogg, and explained the unprecedented difficulties of the industry owing to the high cost of rubber, which is attributed to British restrictions though it is not alleged that there is unfair discrimination against America especially.
Mr. Kellogg promised to consider a "memorial left on behalf of the Rubber Association.

Warsaw, July 18.—After an exciting, Wild-West type of chase in motor cars through the main streets, the Police captured three Communists in the outskirts of the city. Two Police and one Communist were killed and fourteen pedestrians and the remaining two Communists wounded.—Reuter.

Press despatches from Korea carry news of a repetition of floods in the neighbourhood of Seoul owing to three days of rain. Railway traffic is suspended in Seoul and the water supply cut off. Many casualties are feared, while property damage is extensive.

Communications with Seoul are apparently completely severed. Reports as they come through state that the river rose some thirty-six feet in the suburb of Ryuzan, breaking down embankments and flooding everywhere. The City is without light, water and gas.
